queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its hollow lower trunk and cut-back limbs, propped and ringed with metal, turning a dense cone of gold each November. It stands beside the Gion Yamakasa starting point at Kushida Shrine.
queue.story: A 1913 stone monument at the foot of this ginkgo already declared it over a thousand years old, and the monument itself is now old enough to be doubted along with the tree. A later measurement of its trunk put the real figure closer to 600 years, which barely dents the point: this is Hakata's most sung-about tree, its own line in the centuries-old Hakata Iwai Uta, the toast still performed at weddings and shop openings across the district. It stands beside the starting point of the Gion Yamakasa festival, so its crown has watched every decorated float lurch past below it every July for generations. queue.recognise: You can recognise them by the three large ginkgos standing together opposite the main hall, a few steps from the shrine's more famous single ginkgo. They stand at Kushida Shrine.
queue.story: On the fifth of October, seven priests climb in with bamboo poles and shake this tree until the nuts come down. Shrine maidens gather them with chopsticks, because ginkgo flesh smells strongly enough that nobody wants it on their hands, and the nuts are dried and kept until March, when they are given out at the Ginan Festival as charms for a harmonious marriage and for children. That is the whole reason these trees carry their name. They stand opposite the main hall, three large ginkgos of over three hundred years treated as a single married pair, and the one at the front is the female that actually fruits.
